objectiveAlignments.objective: Understand and compare major software development lifecycle models and their applicability
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 4-6 exceed expectations by requiring risk-driven evaluation and critique of SDLC models rather than just comparison. Slide 4 demands failure mode analysis and assumption critique. Slide 6 requires custom SDLC design with risk mitigation justification, demonstrating evaluate-level engagement with model selection.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Apply quality assurance principles and testing strategies to ensure software reliability
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 7-9 systematically address this objective at higher cognitive levels. Slide 7 requires critiquing and redesigning QA budget allocation using cost-benefit analysis. Slide 8 demands evaluation of inverted test pyramid and redesign with defect prediction. Slide 9 requires assessing test suite quality using mutation scores and designing targeted improvements. Activities move beyond application to quality assessment and strategic redesign.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Implement configuration management and version control practices in team environments
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 10-12 directly address implementation through hands-on activities. Slide 10 requires resolving merge conflicts and writing Git commands with workflow justification. Slide 11 evaluates branching strategies with risk analysis. Slide 12 applies semantic versioning to fix dependency issues. Slide 16 synthesizes configuration practices into complete workflow design. Strong alignment with implementation focus.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Design and deploy continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 13-14 directly target pipeline design at create level. Slide 13 requires designing optimized CI pipeline architecture with parallelization strategy, quality gates, and resource trade-offs. Slide 14 demands multi-scenario evaluation of deployment strategies with failure mode mitigation. Both activities require synthesizing stages, gates, and constraints into cohesive architectures rather than applying templates.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Select and apply appropriate software metrics to measure quality and progress
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 15-16 address metrics through GQM application. Slide 15 requires operationalizing GQM by deriving questions, selecting concrete metrics with measurement procedures, and specifying targets. Includes Goodhart's Law critique to prevent naive application. Slide 16 integrates metrics into complete workflow design. Strong alignment with selection and application of measurement strategies.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Synthesize OO principles, design patterns, contracts, and agile methods into cohesive development practices
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 1, 3, 6, and 16 systematically build synthesis capability. Slide 1 opens with create-level quality architecture design requiring integration of 4+ course concepts without scaffolding. Slide 3 demands workflow design integrating SDLC, testing, branching, CI/CD, and metrics. Slide 6 requires custom SDLC synthesis addressing specific failure modes. Slide 16 culminates with complete workflow design integrating all course concepts for healthcare compliance scenario. Strong synthesis thread throughout deck.

slideTags.slideTitle: Software Engineering Process and Quality Assurance
slideTags.evidence: Opening activity requires designing complete quality improvement strategy integrating 4+ course concepts without framework scaffolding. Students must justify integration architecture and explain how combination creates cohesive quality assurance. No structured guidance provided—pure synthesis from scratch.

Activity requires mapping quality attributes to three-pillar framework, identifying which practices support each attribute. Moves beyond understanding framework to analyzing how multiple pillars contribute to each quality dimension. Bridges conceptual model to actionable practices.

slideTags.slideTitle: Integration Challenge: Design Your Development Workflow
slideTags.evidence: Requires designing cohesive workflow integrating SDLC model, testing strategy, branching strategy, CI/CD stages, and metrics for safety-critical medical device scenario. Students must justify each choice considering regulatory constraints, team composition, and safety requirements. Pure synthesis activity.

slideTags.slideTitle: Traditional SDLC Models: Evaluation and Risk Analysis
slideTags.evidence: Demands evaluation of three SDLC models across three scenarios using risk mitigation effectiveness, assumption validity, failure mode severity, and cost-benefit criteria. Requires critiquing when model assumptions break and assessing which risks each model overlooks. Explicit evaluate-level engagement.

slideTags.slideTitle: Agile and Iterative Models: Comparative Analysis
slideTags.evidence: Requires comparative analysis of Scrum vs Kanban frameworks, analyzing trade-offs between sprint commitment and flow-based delivery. Students must justify hybrid approach addressing both predictability and flow efficiency. Systematic comparison with trade-off analysis.

Requires designing custom SDLC by evaluating how specific practices address failure modes. Students must analyze trade-offs where design choices create new risks and specify mitigation strategies. Risk-driven design requiring evaluation of practice effectiveness against specific failure scenarios.

Requires critiquing existing QA budget allocation using cost-of-quality framework, assessing adequacy against reliability requirements, and redesigning investment strategy. Students must judge misalignment between investment and defect economics, then synthesize improved allocation with predicted impact justification.

Demands critique of inverted test pyramid distribution, assessment of adequacy for reliability requirements, and redesign specifying test counts per level with mutation coverage and defect reduction predictions. Requires judging test suite quality against multiple criteria and synthesizing improved strategy.

Requires critiquing test suite quality using coverage vs mutation score gap, assessing adequacy for mission-critical requirements, identifying untested contract properties, and designing targeted tests with explicit property-to-mutant mappings. Multi-dimensional quality assessment with strategic improvement design.

slideTags.slideTitle: Version Control with Git: Team Implementation
slideTags.evidence: Requires resolving realistic merge conflict by writing integrated code, executing proper Git commands with conventional commit message, and proposing workflow practice to prevent future conflicts. Hands-on implementation of version control practices in team context.

slideTags.slideTitle: Branching Strategies: Risk Analysis and Selection
slideTags.evidence: Requires ranking three branching strategies across two scenarios, identifying top failure modes given team constraints, and proposing mitigation for primary risks. Students must judge strategy appropriateness by evaluating how team characteristics amplify or mitigate failure modes across multiple dimensions.

Requires diagnosing risky dependency specifications causing non-reproducible builds and applying semantic versioning principles to fix configuration. Students must decide exact vs range versioning, justify lock file usage, and propose update strategy. Problem-solving through principle application.

Requires designing optimized CI pipeline architecture specifying stage parallelization, quality gate placement, and resource trade-offs to achieve <10min feedback. Students must synthesize pipeline stages, testing strategy, and constraints into cohesive solution with justified stage ordering and failure handling.

Requires evaluating three deployment strategies across three scenarios against risk, compliance, and operational criteria. Students must rank strategies with specific justification, identify critical failure modes, design mitigation, and critique why lowest-ranked strategy would fail. Multi-scenario comparative assessment.

Requires operationalizing GQM by deriving questions, selecting concrete metrics with measurement procedures, specifying target values, and identifying gaming risks. Students must apply GQM framework to production incident reduction goal with practical metric selection and threshold specification.

Requires designing complete development workflow integrating branching strategy, TDD/CI/CD pipeline with quality gates, GQM-derived metrics, and contract enforcement for HIPAA compliance. Students must synthesize all course concepts into justified workflow addressing healthcare regulatory constraints and velocity requirements.

Reviews course journey through three-pillar framework showing how construction, architecture, and engineering concepts integrate. Primarily explanatory content connecting course modules without demanding higher-order cognitive work from students.

Presents professional competency model and next steps for continued learning. Primarily informational content about career development without cognitive demand beyond comprehension of professional development pathways.

gaps: Limited explicit remember/understand content for foundational concepts. Students encountering SDLC models, testing strategies, or Git workflows for first time may struggle with immediate evaluate-level demands without conceptual scaffolding.

Slide 2's three-pillar framework introduced at understand level but immediately leveraged for analyze-level mapping. Consider brief remember-level review of OO principles, patterns, and DbC from prior lectures before demanding integration.

Mutation testing (slide 9) introduced as new concept within evaluate-level activity. Students unfamiliar with mutation scores may struggle to critique test suite quality without prior understand-level explanation of what mutation testing measures.
No explicit scaffolding between slides 1 and 3's create-level synthesis activities. Students may benefit from intermediate apply-level practice integrating 2-3 concepts before full workflow design.
Slides 17-18 drop to understand level after sustained evaluate/create demands. Consider capstone create-level activity synthesizing entire course rather than passive review.
suggestions: Add 2-minute conceptual primer before slide 4's SDLC evaluation activity. Briefly review Waterfall/V-Model/Spiral characteristics at remember level before demanding risk analysis, especially for students without prior software engineering coursework.

Strengthen slide 9 by adding brief understand-level explanation of mutation testing mechanics before critique activity. Show example mutant and how tests kill it, then transition to quality assessment exercise.

Consider reordering slides 1-3 to scaffold synthesis progression: Move slide 2's framework introduction before slide 1's opening activity, allowing students to leverage three-pillar structure in their initial quality architecture design.

Replace slide 17's passive review with active synthesis: Provide complex scenario requiring students to trace how construction principles enable architectural patterns which are validated through engineering processes. Demand explicit connection-making rather than concept listing.

Add metacognitive reflection prompts throughout evaluate/create activities: 'What criteria are you using to judge this trade-off?' or 'How does this design decision constrain future choices?' Make evaluation reasoning explicit.

Strengthen slide 18 by adding create-level capstone: 'Design your personal learning roadmap integrating technical, process, and professional skills for your target role (e.g., backend engineer, DevOps specialist). Justify skill sequencing and identify knowledge dependencies.' Maintains high cognitive demand through conclusion.

Consider adding brief apply-level Git command practice before slide 11's branching strategy evaluation. Students may struggle evaluating workflow risks without hands-on experience with merge conflicts and branch management.

Slide 6's custom SDLC design could benefit from worked example showing how one practice addresses specific failure mode. Provide 1-2 minute demonstration of risk-driven design reasoning before pairs attempt full synthesis.

Add explicit connection between slides 7-9's quality assessment activities and slide 15's metrics. Show how mutation scores, coverage gaps, and defect rates become GQM metrics for quality goals. Strengthen vertical integration across quality assurance sequence.

Consider adding analyze-level activity comparing student-generated solutions after create-level exercises. Have pairs exchange workflow designs (slides 3, 13, 16) and critique each other's integration logic, making synthesis reasoning explicit through peer evaluation.
